name: Hardcore Punk
about: Hardcore is what American teenagers did to punk between 1979 and 1982: faster, shorter, louder and stripped of any art-school ambiguity. It took root in Washington, D.C. around Bad Brains and Ian MacKaye's Minor Threat, in Southern California around Black Flag and the Circle Jerks, and in San Francisco, Boston and Detroit, with Discharge providing the British equivalent. The songs run a minute or two, the drums are a blur, the vocals are barked, and the records were pressed by the bands themselves on labels like Dischord and SST. Straight edge, all-ages shows and hand-drawn flyers came with it. New York's youth crew refined it in the late 1980s; Converge and Refused stretched it in the 1990s; Fucked Up and Turnstile have carried it into the wider world since.

artists.name: Black Flag
artists.why: SST, the van and the relentless tour

artists.name: Bad Brains
artists.why: the fastest, most musical hardcore band

artists.name: Minor Threat
artists.why: Ian MacKaye, Dischord and straight edge

artists.name: Dead Kennedys
artists.why: Jello Biafra's satire at full speed

artists.name: Hüsker Dü
artists.why: took hardcore somewhere melodic and vast

albums.title: Fresh Fruit for Rotting Vegetables
albums.why: Jello Biafra's warbling satire over East Bay Ray's surf-twang guitar made the funniest, sharpest and most durable American punk debut.

albums.title: Group Sex
albums.why: Fourteen songs in under sixteen minutes from Keith Morris after Black Flag, the record that set hardcore's tempo and its sense of humor.

albums.title: Damaged
albums.why: Henry Rollins's first album with the band, pulled by its label for being anti-parent, is the sound of hardcore's rage becoming an aesthetic.

albums.title: Adolescents
albums.why: The Orange County teenagers' blue album paired Rikk Agnew's melodic guitar with Kids of the Black Hole, and suburban hardcore had its anthem.

albums.title: Bad Brains
albums.why: The ROIR cassette caught the Washington quartet at full speed, with Banned in D.C. and Pay to Cum setting a bar for hardcore nobody cleared.

albums.title: Hear Nothing See Nothing Say Nothing
albums.why: Anti-war slogans shouted over a single drum pattern at a single speed, the British record that invented d-beat and shook thrash metal into being.

albums.title: Plastic Surgery Disasters
albums.why: Faster and darker than the debut, with D.H. Lawrence Peckinpah's Moon Over Marin and Terminal Preppie, it is the band's most complete album.

albums.title: Faith/Void
albums.why: Dischord's split LP paired Alec MacKaye's tight Faith with Void's chaotic, proto-metal noise, and the Void side has influenced everyone since.

albums.title: Out of Step
albums.why: Ian MacKaye's band stretched out slightly on its only twelve-inch, and the title track's straight-edge creed still defines a subculture.

albums.title: Tied Down
albums.why: John Brannon's bellow and the Detroit band's only full-length gave hardcore its meanest, most Oi!-influenced sound and a thousand imitators.

albums.title: Rock for Light
albums.why: Ric Ocasek produced the studio re-recordings of the cassette's songs plus new ones, with the reggae cuts and H.R.'s voice cleaner and no less fierce.

albums.title: Suicidal Tendencies
albums.why: Institutionalized and Mike Muir's Venice gang persona brought skate culture and the first hints of thrash crossover into hardcore's biggest early seller.

albums.title: My War
albums.why: The sludgy, Sabbath-paced second side alienated hardcore kids and planted grunge, sludge and stoner rock; the first side is the band at its angriest.

albums.title: Double Nickels on the Dime
albums.why: Forty-five short songs of funk, jazz, folk and politics from San Pedro, the record that showed punk could be about anything and played any way.

albums.title: Zen Arcade
albums.why: A hardcore double concept album with piano interludes, acoustic songs and a fourteen-minute closer, it mapped the route from punk to alternative rock.

albums.title: Victim in Pain
albums.why: Roger Miret and Vinnie Stigma's eleven songs in fifteen minutes defined New York hardcore's skinhead-adjacent sound and its sense of neighborhood loyalty.

albums.title: The Crew
albums.why: Kevin Seconds's positive, singalong Reno hardcore on the band's first full album became the template for youth crew and melodic hardcore alike.

albums.title: The Age of Quarrel
albums.why: Harley Flanagan and John Joseph's Hare Krishna street hardcore with metal riffs made the New York scene's definitive record and crossover thrash's model.

albums.title: Break Down the Walls
albums.why: Ray Cappo's straight-edge revival and the gang vocals on the title song defined youth crew, a scene that still dresses and sounds like this.

albums.title: Start Today
albums.why: Walter Schreifels's melodic songs and Civ's shout made the youth crew's most tuneful record, the one that aged best and pointed toward post-hardcore.

albums.title: Feel the Darkness
albums.why: Portland's self-styled kings of punk delivered their heaviest, most rock-and-roll album, with Plastic Bomb and Alan's on Fire the hardcore-metal peak.

albums.title: Jane Doe
albums.why: Jacob Bannon's screams and Kurt Ballou's production on a breakup record of mathematical violence made the album metallic hardcore is still measured against.

albums.title: The Chemistry of Common Life
albums.why: Damian Abraham's bark over layered guitars, flutes and bongos won the Toronto band the Polaris Prize and proved hardcore could sprawl.

albums.title: Glow On
albums.why: Baltimore hardcore with dream-pop, funk and Blood Orange cameos, it became the rare punk record to cross over without softening.
